clue.text: An official has to stand behind it! Run across it and it goes up on the board.

definitions.text: An official has to stand behind it!
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the baseball umpire crouches behind this spot to call pitches

definitions.text: Run across it and it goes up on the board
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a runner crossing it scores a run, posted on the scoreboard

explanation.surface: Sounds like a riddle about a referee and a noticeboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves describe the same spot on a baseball diamond: the umpire stands behind it, and a runner crossing it scores.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball, the umpire calls pitches from behind this base, and a run counts when a runner touches it.

clue.text: Earth-shaking type of courage!

definitions.text: type of courage!

indicators.note: shaking means the letters of earth are jumbled into another word

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Praise for bravery so great it moves the ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Heart is a byword for bravery, as in 'take heart' or 'have the heart to try'.

clue.text: Melodic embellishment in your private nook, when little Mortimer is around.

definitions.text: Melodic embellishment

indicators.note: around says the short name goes around the nook, which sits inside it

parts.note: Mort is the short form of the name Mortimer
a den is a private room or nook

explanation.surface: A musical flourish played in your study while a boy called Mortimer is nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: A mordent is a musical ornament: a quick alternation between a written note and the one next to it.

clue.text: Bob is at one end of such, used if you like things straight up and down.

definitions.text: Bob is at one end of such
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a plumb bob is the weight hanging at the bottom of the cord

definitions.text: used if you like things straight up and down
definitions.meaning: second meaning: builders hang them to check that walls are truly vertical

explanation.walkthrough: Bob reads as a man's name; here it is the weight on a string.
explanation.definitionFit: A weighted cord hangs exactly vertical under gravity, so builders and decorators use it to find the true upright.

clue.text: A golf club, when in the sand, possibly. (Fire back on them!)

definitions.text: Fire back on them!

indicators.note: when in places the golf club inside the rearranged sand
possibly means the letters of sand are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged
an iron is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: A golfer's iron dropped in a bunker, and a call to shoot back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire back' sounds like returning gunfire; it means the fire leans back on these metal supports.
explanation.definitionFit: These paired metal stands hold logs in a fireplace, so the fire rests on them.

clue.text: The wrong name otherwise–a charming one might do it.

definitions.text: a charming one might do it

indicators.note: the word name is set wrong, its letters out of order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged
or means otherwise, as in 'hurry, or else'

explanation.surface: Calling someone by the wrong name, though a charmer might get away with it.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the American spelling, without the U.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamor is to captivate someone, which is just what a charming person can do.

clue.text: Cause a couple of hands to get together, and go up and down.

definitions.text: Cause a couple of hands to get together
definitions.meaning: first meaning: to ... hands is to bring two people's hands together

definitions.text: go up and down
definitions.meaning: second meaning: to move quickly up and down

explanation.walkthrough: The first half sounds like organizing applause or a team of farm hands; it is the handshake sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both a greeting, where two hands are joined, and a rapid jolting motion back and forth.

clue.text: To which carts were pulled by hand, and someone finally said, "This is the place!"

definitions.text: To which carts were pulled by hand, and someone finally said, "This is the place!"

parts.words: To which carts were pulled by hand
parts.note: Mormon handcart pioneers hauled their belongings west across the plains in the 1850s

parts.words: someone finally said, "This is the place!"
parts.note: Brigham Young's words on first seeing the valley in 1847

explanation.surface: A history quiz about a journey made with handcarts that ended with a famous declaration.
explanation.walkthrough: Brigham Young led the Mormon settlers there, and 'This is the place' is the phrase linked to the founding.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mormon capital was founded where Brigham Young stopped, and handcart companies later trekked there from Iowa.

clue.text: A place in Massachusetts also finished here.

definitions.text: A place in Massachusetts

parts.note: and adds something, meaning also
over means finished, as in 'the game is over'

explanation.surface: A New England town where something also came to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is home to Phillips Academy; 'here' is a link at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Andover is a town in northeastern Massachusetts, north of Boston.

clue.text: Stop those feelings of rage! Such causes possible harm!

definitions.text: causes possible harm!

parts.note: to end something is to stop it
angers are feelings of rage

explanation.surface: A plea to control outbursts of fury because they do damage.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger is to put something at risk, so it brings the chance of harm without making harm certain.

clue.text: One doesn't like to run it when sailing.

definitions.text: One doesn't like to run it when sailing.

parts.words: One doesn't like to run it
parts.note: read as a race or errand someone dislikes, but it completes the idiom 'run ___', meaning to strike the bottom
places it at sea, where a vessel can hit the shallows

explanation.surface: Seems to be about a sailor who dislikes running some course or errand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' stands for the answer word itself, completing the phrase for a ship striking the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A vessel that runs onto the seabed or shore is stuck, which no sailor wants.

clue.text: Made reference to the fact that everything gets sort of due, with a barely passing grade.

definitions.text: Made reference

parts.note: all means everything

indicators.note: something only sort of due is a rough, reworked version of the word due

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged
D is the lowest passing letter grade in American schools

explanation.surface: A teacher making a point about overdue homework and a scraped pass mark.
explanation.walkthrough: In US schools D is the lowest grade that still passes, below A, B and C.
explanation.definitionFit: To allude is to mention something indirectly, so made reference is an exact synonym in the past tense.

clue.text: 6 across could get 30, to a point, and earn this title.

definitions.text: 6 across could get 30, to a point, and earn this title.

parts.words: 6 across could get 30, to a point
parts.note: 6 across is SHAKE and 30 across is SPEAR; together they almost spell the playwright's surname, missing only its final E
the title is the playwright's nickname, taken from his birthplace on the river

explanation.surface: A cross-reference puzzle that sounds like scoring points to win a championship title.
explanation.walkthrough: SHAKE plus SPEAR gives Shakespear, which is the playwright's name 'to a point', short of its last letter. Stratford-upon-Avon was his birthplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare is traditionally called this, a bard being a poet and the Avon the river at his home town.

clue.text: See 11
See 11
The Mikado, for example.

definitions.text: The Mikado, for example.

parts.note: the Mikado is a title of the Japanese emperor, but also a Gilbert and Sullivan work
flags that the work is one instance of a genre

explanation.walkthrough: The Mikado suggests an emperor or Japan; it is also the 1885 Gilbert and Sullivan stage work.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbert and Sullivan's Mikado is a humorous stage work with spoken dialogue and songs, the type of light musical theater named here.

clue.text: One of these digs in the sand and lies in wait for the worker going to Long Island briefly, meeting a disturbed offspring.

definitions.text: One of these digs in the sand and lies in wait

parts.note: a worker is a worker ant
LI is the usual short form of Long Island, New York

indicators.note: disturbed means the letters of the son are stirred into a new order

parts.note: a son is offspring

explanation.surface: An unlikely tale of a commuter to Long Island meeting a troubled child, after a predator in the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'These' in the definition makes the answer plural. The insect larva digs a pit in sand and waits at the bottom for ants to fall in.
explanation.definitionFit: The larva of this insect excavates a funnel-shaped trap in sandy ground and ambushes prey that slips in.

clue.text: Tells everyone that the young lady has put on a little weight!

definitions.text: Tells everyone

indicators.note: put on means the small weight goes onto the girl, joining her name and her 's

parts.note: Ann is a girl's name
the 's in 'she's done' stands for has
an ounce is a small unit of weight

explanation.surface: Gossip that a girl has gained a little weight.
explanation.definitionFit: To announce something is to make it public, so it tells everyone at once.

clue.text: In public, ours expect to show where drivers start out at least nine times–and swear about nothing at all!

definitions.text: where drivers start out at least nine times

indicators.note: In tells the solver the answer lies inside the next few words
to show says those words put the answer on display

parts.note: the run of letters straddles public, ours and expect

explanation.surface: A puzzling sentence mixing public expectations, motorists setting out, and bad language.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue doubles its wordplay: the tail also gives CURSE (swear) around O (nothing). Drivers are golf clubs, used from the tee at each of at least nine holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf course has nine or eighteen holes, and golfers usually tee off with a driver at each one.

clue.text: See 6
Where they feel low-down, even at home? Remainder the lady's property!

definitions.text: Where they feel low-down, even at home?

parts.note: net is what remains after deductions
her is the possessive for a woman
lands are property, real estate

explanation.surface: A woman's estate, left as the remainder of an inheritance, and someone feeling down at home.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pun: the country's name means 'low lands', so its people are low-down even at home.
explanation.definitionFit: The country's name literally means lower lands, as much of it lies below sea level.

clue.text: A flying one might be associated with the air.

definitions.text: A flying one might be associated with the air.

parts.note: reads as any airborne thing, but it is the acrobat's swinging bar in an old music-hall song about a daring young man
air means a tune, though it seems to mean the sky an acrobat swings through

explanation.surface: A circus act high up in the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' reads as the space above the ring, but it is also a song: the 1867 tune 'The Daring Young Man on the Flying Trapeze'.
explanation.definitionFit: A swinging bar for acrobats, the flying version is famous from a popular 19th-century song.

clue.text: They're hailed more often than Caesar was!

definitions.text: They're hailed more often than Caesar was!

parts.note: read as being saluted, but hailing here is waving down a ride in the street
recalls the Roman salute 'Hail, Caesar!'

explanation.surface: A joke comparing something greeted constantly with the Roman emperor's famous salutes.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface steers toward celebrities or rulers; the city vehicles are hailed far more often than any emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: City cabs are summoned by a raised arm or shout, so passengers hail them many times every day.

clue.text: A plant of the buttercup family, done to a nice turn.

definitions.text: A plant of the buttercup family

indicators.note: done in the cooking sense: the letters are cooked into a new form
done to a turn means cooked just right, and the turn also signals the letters of 'to a nice' being turned around

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A plant that has been cooked perfectly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Done to a turn' is the cooking idiom for perfectly cooked.
explanation.definitionFit: Aconite, also called monkshood or wolfsbane, is a poisonous flowering plant in the buttercup family, Ranunculaceae.

clue.text: A glorious day to many–and part of our thoughts show it!

definitions.text: A glorious day to many

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters sitting inside the words 'of our thoughts'

parts.note: the answer runs across the end of of, all of our and the start of thoughts

explanation.surface: A splendid day for many people, which our thoughts reflect.
explanation.walkthrough: Americans call Independence Day, July 4, 'the Glorious Fourth'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fourth of July, US Independence Day, is traditionally called the Glorious Fourth, a holiday for millions.

clue.text: See 6 down
Also dragged around inside in Spain?

definitions.text: in Spain?
definitions.note: short for 'a place in Spain': the question mark admits the answer is one example

indicators.note: the word for also goes around the other word, which ends up inside it

parts.note: too means also
led, as one is led or dragged along by the hand

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a thing was also hauled around indoors in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only 'in Spain?', standing for a place there; the question mark flags that it is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The historic city, famous for its swords, is in central Spain, so it is one place there.

clue.text: Possibly low flying at night, traditionally.

definitions.text: Possibly low flying at night, traditionally.

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of low may be rearranged into another word

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Something might be flying low through the dark, as it customarily does.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a rearranged 'low' gives the bird that traditionally hunts at night.
explanation.definitionFit: The nocturnal bird of prey is the traditional emblem of night flight, often skimming low over fields.

clue.text: See 18 across
The main part comes up with deserters from the ship.

definitions.text: The main part

indicators.note: in a down entry, comes up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: rats are said to desert a sinking ship

explanation.surface: The bulk of a ship's crew comes on deck along with those abandoning it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main part' sounds like most of something; it is the leading role in a show. 'Main' also hints at the sea, adding to the ship surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The star of a play or film takes the lead role, the principal part in the production.

clue.text: One who doesn't play fair makes a bad teacher.

definitions.text: One who doesn't play fair

indicators.note: a bad version of the word teacher is a corrupted rearrangement of its letters

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dishonest person would make a poor schoolteacher.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cheats breaks the rules of a game or test to win, so does not play fair.

clue.text: I exist in a rainstorm finally, like the Spanish or Portuguese.

definitions.text: like the Spanish or Portuguese

indicators.note: finally says the rearranged rain comes last, after the first two pieces

parts.note: taken as written
be means exist
split as rain plus storm: rain with its letters stormed, or tossed about, gives these letters

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a downpour, apparently living like people from Spain or Portugal.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis splits rainstorm into its parts: rain is the fodder and storm the signal, with 'in a' joining. The peninsula holding Spain and Portugal is called Iberia.
explanation.definitionFit: Spain and Portugal share the Iberian peninsula, so anything typical of their peoples is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Perhaps stick with a fork in reaching for the asparagus, in part–or possibly pears, too!

definitions.text: Perhaps stick with a fork

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of pears might be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Dinner-table advice on spearing asparagus, or pears, with a fork.
explanation.walkthrough: A middle hint adds a third route: an asparagus stalk is called a spear, the part of the vegetable you reach for.
explanation.definitionFit: To spear food is to pierce and lift it with a pointed implement such as a fork's prongs.

clue.text: Swingers of a sort make them at times. (They reputedly work only in the sunshine!)

definitions.text: Swingers of a sort make them at times
definitions.meaning: first meaning: wild, swinging punches thrown by boxers

definitions.text: They reputedly work only in the sunshine!
definitions.meaning: second meaning: people making hay, who proverbially make it while the sun shines

explanation.walkthrough: The first half points at dancers or playground swings; the swingers are boxers. The second half plays on the proverb 'make hay while the sun shines'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both big roundhouse punches in boxing and farm workers who cut and dry grass for fodder.
